summary: GDOI lets a group key server push new security associations to group members, for example to rekey. This memo adds the ability for the server to ask each member to send back an acknowledgement, so the server knows who actually received the update.

eli5.summary: When a teacher hands out new instructions, she asks everyone to nod back so she knows they all got them.

questions: how does gdoi acknowledge rekey messages
how does a gcks know group members got a rekey
what is the groupkey-push ack hash
subtitle: How a group member tells a GDOI key server that it received and applied a rekey message.

tldr.problem: A GDOI Group Controller/Key Server pushes new policy and keys to group members, but normally never learns whether each member actually received them.
tldr.mechanism: The server adds a KEK_ACK_REQUESTED attribute to the group's policy. Members then reply to each GROUPKEY-PUSH with an acknowledgement carrying the push's sequence number and the member's identity, authenticated by a keyed hash.
tldr.outcome: The server can tell which members are getting current policy and which may have left. Implementing the acknowledgement is OPTIONAL.

facts.label: GCKS minimum wait before ACK is missing

today: RFC 8263 is a Proposed Standard from November 2017. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why Acknowledge a Rekey
sections.content:
The Group Domain of Interpretation (GDOI, RFC 6407) is a group key management method. A Group Controller/Key Server (GCKS) distributes security associations, meaning cryptographic policy and keying material, to Group Member (GM) devices. Its Rekey Protocol is the GROUPKEY-PUSH message, which can carry new, replacement or deleted policy and keys.

Usually the GCKS does not need to know that a GM got the message. Sometimes it helps: a GCKS policy can use acknowledgements to work out which GMs are receiving current policy and which are no longer participating.

This memo defines the GROUPKEY-PUSH Acknowledgement Message. The GCKS first asks for acknowledgements as part of the group policy, and each GM that honors the request replies to every GROUPKEY-PUSH. Implementing the acknowledgement is OPTIONAL.
sections.eli5: A teacher sends new rules to a class. Usually she does not check who read them. Here she asks each student to send a quick note back saying they got the rules.

sections.title: Requesting Acknowledgements
sections.content:
When a GM joins, it contacts the GCKS with a GROUPKEY-PULL registration. If the group uses GROUPKEY-PUSH, the downloaded policy includes an SA KEK payload that tells the GM how it will receive rekey messages. To request acknowledgements, the GCKS adds a new KEK attribute, KEK_ACK_REQUESTED (value 9), to that SA KEK policy.

The attribute's value selects one of four types. They share one message format but differ in the pseudorandom function (prf) and in the base_key from which the acknowledgement key is derived:

  • REKEY_ACK_KEK_SHA256: used when the KEK Download Type is part of the policy. The prf is PRF-HMAC-SHA-256 and the base_key is the KEK_ALGORITHM_KEY used to decrypt the GROUPKEY-PUSH message, without any explicit IV.
  • REKEY_ACK_LKH_SHA256: used when the KEK management algorithm is Logical Key Hierarchy (LKH). The base_key is the Key Data of the first LKH Key structure in the LKH_DOWNLOAD_ARRAY, a secret the GCKS shares with that one GM.
  • REKEY_ACK_KEK_SHA512 and REKEY_ACK_LKH_SHA512: identical to the SHA256 types except that the prf is PRF-HMAC-SHA-512.
sections.eli5: The teacher writes on the rules sheet: please send a note back, and here is the secret handshake to use. There are four kinds of handshake, which differ in the secret used and in how strong the scrambling is.

sections.title: The Acknowledgement Message
sections.content:
The acknowledgement has four payloads: HDR, HASH, SEQ, ID. It is built like a reply: addresses and UDP ports of the GROUPKEY-PUSH are swapped, with the GM using its own IP address as the source.

  • HDR: follows the GROUPKEY-PUSH header of RFC 6407. The cookies are copied from the push message and act as a Security Parameter Index. Next Payload is Hash (value 8), Major Version is 1, Minor Version is 0, Exchange Type is 35, Flags are 0 and Message ID MUST be 0.
  • HASH: HASH = prf(ack_key, SEQ | ID). The ack_key is derived with a key derivation function in feedback mode (NIST SP800-108) as prf(base_key, "GROUPKEY-PUSH ACK" | SPI | L), where SPI is the Initiator Cookie followed by the Responder Cookie and L is the key length in bits as two octets in network byte order.
  • SEQ: the sequence number copied from the GROUPKEY-PUSH message.
  • ID: the GM's identity as ID_IPV4_ADDR, ID_IPV6_ADDR or ID_OID. Protocol ID and Port MUST be 0, and the address MUST match the source IP address of the most recent GROUPKEY-PULL exchange.
sections.eli5: The reply note has a stamp copied from the original, the number of the message being answered, who is answering, and a secret signature that only real group members can make.

sections.title: Member and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A GM that sees KEK_ACK_REQUESTED in an SA KEK, from either a GROUPKEY-PULL or a GROUPKEY-PUSH, records that it is expected to acknowledge. A GM that recognizes the attribute MUST honor it, because the GCKS may act on unresponsive members, including no longer sending them GROUPKEY-PUSH messages. If a GM cannot send the requested type, it still continues in the group. After successfully processing a push, the GM sends the ACK, even if the push deletes the KEK that protected it.

The GCKS includes the attribute every time it delivers the SA KEK. On receiving an ACK, it first checks that group policy calls for ACKs, otherwise discarding the message. It SHOULD keep a record, such as a hash, of recent ACKs to reject duplicates before doing cryptographic work. It then validates the format and the HASH, discards the message if either fails, and records that this GM received the push with that sequence number.
sections.eli5: A student who got the rules must send the note back, even if the new rules cancel the old ones. The teacher ignores notes that look wrong or that she has already seen, and ticks off each student who sent a good one.

sections.title: Management Considerations
sections.content:
An acknowledgement is one more way for a GCKS to judge whether a GM is live, but a rekey or ACK can be lost in the network, so a missing ACK should not be the only factor. A GCKS SHOULD NOT consider a GM to have left the group until it has received at least one ACK from it.

  • A GM receiving a multicast push MAY add jitter to its ACK, but MUST NOT delay it more than 5 seconds.
  • A GCKS SHOULD NOT declare an ACK missing until it has waited at least 10 seconds. Implementations SHOULD make these timers configurable.
  • Missing ACKs SHOULD trigger a logging event. Policy may resend the push several times, alert administrators or remove unresponsive GMs, but a removed GM will not get newer policy until it contacts the GCKS again.
  • If a push deletes the KEK that protected it, the GCKS SHOULD NOT delete that KEK until GMs have had time to acknowledge.
  • A GCKS SHOULD log unexpected, malformed or failed-validation ACKs.
sections.eli5: The teacher should be patient. A note might be slow or lost in the mail, so she waits at least ten seconds, and does not kick someone out of the class until she has heard from them at least once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The ACK is an ISAKMP message (RFC 2408) protected by the HASH payload, an HMAC over the message bytes. It gives message authentication and protection against man-in-the-middle attacks, but no confidentiality: a passive attacker can see the hash, the sequence number and the GM's identity. The RFC argues this gives the attacker no direct value, since without the KEK it cannot forge a GROUPKEY-PUSH.

With the KEK-based types the key is a group secret, so one authorized GM could impersonate another and falsely claim a push was received. The RFC says this adds no threat beyond an attacker withholding pushes from a victim, and the LKH types avoid it by using a pairwise secret between the GCKS and one GM.

A GM sends an ACK only after fully validating the push, including replay protection and the signature, which limits its use in a distributed denial of service attack on the GCKS. A GCKS SHOULD be ready to receive an ACK from every GM and have enough resources, such as receive queue size, to avoid dropping them. How it uses the sequence number and identity is local policy.
sections.eli5: The signature proves a note came from someone in the class, but anyone can read the note. With the shared class secret one student could fake another's note, so a secret shared with just one student is safer.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA added the KEK_ACK_REQUESTED attribute (value 9, a Basic attribute) to the SA KEK Payload Values registry, and a new registry for its values. It also added a registry of GDOI DOI Exchange Types, where GROUPKEY-PUSH-ACK is value 35. Both registries use Specification Required, and 129 to 255 in the ACK type registry is Private Use.
sections.eli5: The official list of codes got new entries, so every device agrees what the acknowledgement types and the message number mean.
